stories.notes: Story has empty acceptance criteria and no existing spec. Live preview in a CMS is a complex feature involving real-time content rendering, state synchronization between editor and preview, iframe sandboxing, and potential SSRF/XSS vectors. openspec must first elaborate requirements and define technical AC; speckit must then harden with testability criteria, security checks, and edge cases (e.g., preview of unpublished content, permission boundaries, error states during preview fetch failures).

agentContributions.notes: Live Preview is a novel capability — the codebase currently fetches only published content. The attachment point is useContent (236 callers), the central hook that resolves content by key. All Contentstack-backed components (ContentstackLink, ContentstackImage, ContentstackTable, ContentstackContentCards, etc.) delegate to useContent, so intercepting it is the minimal-change integration path. Contentstack hosts are unreachable at test time; VCs are written to the boundary of what our code sends/receives.

Openspec produced an empty acceptanceCriteria array with a valuable architectural note about intercepting useContent. I built the full AC list from scratch based on the story title, the key files, and openspec's note. Key design decisions: (1) Contentstack Live Preview uses a URL query parameter to activate and a WebSocket for real-time updates — ACs reflect this standard pattern. (2) AC-2 and AC-8 ensure zero impact on production/non-preview behaviour. (3) AC-7 covers security — invalid/expired tokens must not leak draft content. (4) AC-5 and AC-6 cover connection failure and recovery. (5) AC-9 covers the edge case where an entry has no draft. (6) AC-12 covers nested references, a common Contentstack pattern. (7) AC-13 addresses bundle-size impact — preview code should be tree-shaken out of production builds. (8) AC-16 addresses rapid-update debouncing. (9) AC-17 ensures preview mode survives client-side navigation. (10) AC-18 ensures consistency across the three codebases, noting the casing variant. CAVEAT: I could not read the actual file contents of useContent.ts, ContentstackContext.tsx, contentCard.ts, or ContentstackLink.tsx. If the existing architecture differs significantly from what I assumed (e.g., if useContent already has a preview mechanism, or if the Contentstack SDK version doesn't support WebSockets), some ACs may need adjustment. The ACs are intentionally written as observable outcomes without prescribing implementation, per the what-not-how rule.

coordinatorReview.reviewNotes: All four manifest paths exist (useContent.ts, ContentstackContext.tsx, contentCard.ts, ContentstackLink.tsx) — no missing_manifest_path. Both agents added meaningful, non-overlapping value: openspec identified useContent as the central intercept point (236 callers) and confirmed the codebase currently fetches only published content, providing the architectural anchor; speckit then built a comprehensive verification-criteria set from scratch covering security (invalid/expired tokens), error states (connection failure/recovery), edge cases (no draft, nested references), production isolation, bundle-size tree-shaking, debouncing, and client-side navigation survival. The collaboration pattern is correct. However, speckit explicitly admits it could not read the actual file contents of any of the four manifest files. The entire VC set is constructed on assumptions about the existing architecture — e.g., that useContent has no existing preview mechanism, that the Contentstack SDK supports WebSockets, and that the standard Live Preview query-parameter + WebSocket pattern applies. If any of these assumptions are wrong (useContent already has preview hooks, SDK lacks WebSocket support, or the integration point differs), the verification criteria would be testing for the wrong behaviors. A human must validate the VCs against the actual source of useContent.ts and ContentstackContext.tsx before implementation proceeds. The empty acceptanceCriteria array and acceptanceChanged=false on both agents are expected per brownfield policy and are not defects.
